extracted.intended_audience: journalists and other writers/designers creating infographics for articles
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, journalist-focused guidance for creating inline infographics that communicate one clear idea, support article points, and are shareable. Emphasizes clarity, accuracy, attribution, and appropriate visual style for online news content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Concise
rubrics_metrics.description: Design your infographic to convey one idea really well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You're not writing a scientific research paper, so don't expect your reader to dig into a lot of detail. This doesn't mean you should only visualize one number, but your entire graphic should support one of the major points from the article. You can include additional facts or information to make the infographic stand on its own, but don't lose sight of the point you want to get across. (Example: Caffeine Poster — at a poster size you can tell which drinks have more or less caffeine; higher-resolution image lets readers dig deeper.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Visual
rubrics_metrics.description: Design your infographic with your final viewing size in mind so it can be understood in-line with your article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forcing readers to click a link to view the graphic; design it to be viewable and understandable when embedded in the article. It's acceptable to allow a high-resolution click-through, but the image should be self-contained for inline viewing. A viewable image is also easier to share on social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Smarter
rubrics_metrics.description: Build your data and explanation right into the infographic so readers don't have to work hard to understand it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your infographic shouldn't need a legend to be understandable; avoid making readers move their eyes back and forth between chart and legend. Include relevant descriptions and numbers in the graphic itself. Make the graphic look professional and treat readers as intelligent by providing built-in explanations. (Example: 'Who Participates Online?' by Arno Ghelfi.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Transparent
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite your data sources and allow readers to dig deeper into the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always cite data sources and provide access to source data (for example, links to spreadsheets) so readers can check facts and explore further. Transparency prevents misleading conclusions and builds trust. (Example: BBC Budget — 'See the visual. Explore the data.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Different
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid defaulting to bar, line, or pie charts when another visual form would better express the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a wider range of visualization styles matched to the data type; use resources like the Periodic Table of Visualization to find suitable visuals. Different styles are grouped by the type of data they communicate and examples demonstrate usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Accurate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use correct geometry: visualize differences using area (and ensure visual dimensions are proportional to the values represented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using shapes (e.g., circles) to show relative amounts, ensure the AREA is proportional to the values. For example, making a circle's diameter three times larger creates an area nine times larger. One common exception is a standard bar chart: regardless of bar width, only the bar height should convey magnitude. (Example: Circle Areas; FedEx Universe bubble mind map.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Attractive
rubrics_metrics.description: Include illustrations, photos, and visual affordances that make the infographic quicker and easier to understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual embellishments such as company logos, illustrations, or photos can improve comprehension and visual appeal even when using standard chart types. Attractive design helps readers grasp meaning faster. (Example: Email provider chart with logos.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Varied
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a visual style appropriate to the data and don't be afraid to mix visualization styles within one infographic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the data concerns geographic entities, consider a map rather than a bar chart; mixing maps, stacked bars, colored percentage boxes, etc., is acceptable when it improves clarity. Consider viewing size: visuals should be understandable at article size, with detailed numbers available in high-resolution versions. (Example: Haiti Earthquake infographic mixing map and stacked bar.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Gracious
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume your infographic will be viewed or shared independently from the original article and include metadata and rights information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the final graphic includes: copyright (terms of use), source data (so anyone can check facts), designer's name (credit the artist/illustrator/programmer/designer), and the original image/article address (so viewers can find the original article).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Creative
rubrics_metrics.description: Use whatever tools you have available to create the infographic; choose tools appropriate to the visualization need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools depend on the visualization goal: vector drawing programs (OmniGraffle, Visio), charting programs (Microsoft Office, iWork), image editors (Photoshop), or online visualization tools (Tableau Public, Many Eyes, Swivel, Google Public Data Explorer, Gapminder, Wordle, WorldMapper, GunnMap, StatPlanet Map Maker). Use creativity and available software to achieve the design.
